definition: The share of returned results that are right. Structured filters have perfect precision: everything they return matches.
The share of right results that are returned. Synonym expansion raises recall: "power brick" finds chargers the catalogue never calls that.
A fixed query with expected results at each stage, GQ-01 to GQ-09. Each one is a moment in the talk, checked by an integration test.
SQL whose values are sent separately from its text (@brand, @maxPrice), so user input can never change the statement. The trace shows the values beside the SQL, never pasted into it.
The Postgres @> operator: true when one JSON value contains another. Numbers compare as numbers, so {"voltageV": 18} matches 18 but not "18".
Matching the words of a query against the words of documents, after normalising both: lower case, stemming, stop words. Postgres has it built in.
Postgres's searchable form of a document: its lexemes and their positions, each weighted by the field it came from (A for the name down to D for reviews).
Postgres's parsed form of a search: lexemes joined by & (and), | (or) and <-> (followed by). 'power' & 'brick' & 'laptop' needs all three.
A word reduced to its base form for matching: "batteries" becomes batteri. Queries and documents are matched lexeme by lexeme.
Cutting words to a common stem, so "charger" and "chargers" match. It is language-specific: an English stemmer does nothing useful for "cargador".
A very common word, such as "for" or "my", that full-text search drops before matching because it would match almost everything.

The standard keyword ranking formula: term frequency with saturation, inverse document frequency and document length normalisation. Postgres doesn't implement it, so this repo calls its ranking BM25-style.
Postgres's cover-density ranking: it rewards query lexemes that appear often and close together, weighted by field. It has no IDF and no saturation, which is why it is BM25-style, not BM25.
A weight that makes rare words count for more than common ones. Without it, a word like "charger" that appears everywhere counts as much as a rare model number.
A list of numbers (768 here) that a model makes from text, placed so that texts with similar meanings point in similar directions. Vectors from different models can't be compared.
A dense vector has a value in every dimension, like an embedding. A sparse vector is mostly zeros, one dimension per word, like keyword search. Hybrid search combines the two kinds.
1 minus the cosine of the angle between two vectors: 0 means the same direction, and larger means less alike. It is pgvector's <=> operator; cosine similarity is 1 − distance.
Returning the vectors closest to a query vector. There is no threshold: it always returns the nearest ones, however far away they are.
An approximate nearest-neighbour index: a layered graph that finds close vectors quickly by skipping most of them. ef_search trades speed for recall.
A Postgres extension that stores vectors in a column and orders rows by distance, so similarity and SQL filters run in one statement.
A file format for trained models. ONNX Runtime runs the Nomic embedding model locally from .NET, with no Python and no network.
Running keyword and vector search and combining their results, so exact-word matches and meaning matches both count.
Combines ranked lists using only ranks: RRF(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank), with k = 60. 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+2) = 0.03252, so being in both lists matters far more than being 1st or 2nd.
How many results each retriever returns before fusion and rules: 50 here. Retrieve deep, page late, because a rule can only rescue a product that was retrieved.
A model of a domain: its concepts, what they are called and the rules between them. It describes kinds of thing, never individual products; that would be a knowledge graph.
A W3C standard for taxonomies and thesauri: concepts with preferred and alternative labels, linked by broader and narrower.
A tree of categories from broad to narrow: Power › Chargers › Laptop chargers. Here it is a SKOS concept scheme, and products name their categories by notation.
One idea in a SKOS scheme, such as Chargers. It has a notation (chargers) for code, labels for people, and links to broader and narrower concepts.
skos:altLabel, another name for a concept: "power brick" for Chargers. Labels can be in any language ("Cargadores"@es), and hidden labels hold common misspellings.
skos:broader and skos:narrower link a concept to its parent and its children. Laptop chargers is narrower than Chargers, so a search for chargers includes it.
A small SKOS scheme of allowed spec values, such as the connectors usb-c and barrel-5.5mm, with synonyms like "Type-C". Products store the notation, so values compare exactly.
A class-level constraint between product types, such as "a charger's plug must fit the laptop's charging port". It is stated once per pair of types, never per product, and goes one step beyond SKOS.
The product the shopper owns, from the device picker or a device name in the query. Stage 5 checks candidates against it.
A product that is semantically similar but incompatible, like a 45W barrel charger for a laptop that needs 65W over USB-C. Similarity ranks it high; a rule flags it.
A readable text format for RDF. domain-ontology.ttl holds the taxonomy, the value vocabularies and the rules.
The query language for RDF, as SQL is for tables. The API reads labels and rules from the TTL with small .rq queries.
A model that generates text. In Stages 6–7 it writes the answer and the explanation from the evidence Stage 5 found, and its output is checked, not trusted.
Giving an LLM retrieved evidence to answer from, and asking it to cite that evidence. In Stage 6, better retrieval gives better answers.
Splitting long documents such as manuals and PDFs into pieces before embedding them. How you split decides what can be found. Discussed in the talk, not built.
A second, slower model re-orders the top candidates for precision before they reach a user or an LLM. Discussed in the talk, not built.
A model that reads the query and a document together and scores the pair. More accurate than comparing separate embeddings, but too slow to run over a whole catalogue.
A model produces a sparse, keyword-like vector that also scores related words it learned, as BGE-M3's sparse output does. Discussed in the talk, not built.
A W3C language for formal ontologies that a reasoner can draw conclusions from. The step beyond this repo's small rule vocabulary. Discussed in the talk, not built.
A W3C language for validating RDF data against shapes, such as "every laptop has a chargingPort". Where this repo's rules would grow next. Discussed in the talk, not built.

A graph of facts about individual things (this product, that maker) rather than kinds of thing. Useful for multi-hop questions; this repo keeps products in the catalogue instead. Discussed in the talk, not built.

The bounded list an LLM may use in Stages 6–7: up to 5 compatible products, 3 incompatible ones with their reasons, 2 unknown and 5 unchecked, plus the matched concepts and the rules. The trace shows it in full.

A product ID in square brackets, like [PROD-0012], after every claim about a product. When the answer is complete, the API checks each one against the evidence set; one that isn't there is shown as invalid.
The messages sent to an LLM: here a system message with the rules, and a user message with the question and the evidence. Stages 6–7 keep theirs in files and show them in full in the trace.
A one-way stream of text events over an ordinary HTTP response. The answer arrives as meta, delta, final and done events, so the text appears while it is being written.
How long after the request the first piece of generated text arrives. It decides whether an answer feels fast, more than the total time does.
The design of an explanation. Stage 7's prompt leads with the decision, explains the constraint, contrasts with the near miss, and ends with a rule of thumb and a next step.
Stage 7 with Apply pedagogy off: the same answer, evidence, audience and words, through a plain prompt with no teaching structure. It shows what the pedagogy prompt adds.
Who Stage 7 explains for: novice, enthusiast or expert. It changes the words (everyday alternative labels for a novice, spec terms for an expert), not the facts.
